desc:
The union of a set of closed intervals [a, b] is the set of all real numbers that lie in at least one of them. You are given a list of intervals and want to throw away as many as possible without changing the union.

Return the minimum number of intervals you must keep so that their union is exactly the union of the whole list. Intervals that only touch, like [1, 3] and [3, 5], join into one block [1, 5].

intervals = [[1, 4], [2, 3], [3, 7], [6, 9], [12, 15], [13, 14]]  ->  4

The union is [1, 9] together with [12, 15]. Keep [1, 4], [3, 7], [6, 9] and [12, 15].
constraints: Intervals may repeat or contain each other
hints: Merging the intervals gives the blocks of the union. You need a cover for each block, and different blocks never help each other.
Inside one block, think of covering it from left to right: at each step you need an interval that starts at or before the point already covered and reaches as far as possible.

Sort by start. Keep reach. Scan all intervals with a ≤ reach for the largest end; if that is larger than reach, keep one interval and move reach there. When no progress is possible, the block is finished and the next interval starts a new block.
editorial: Blocks of the union are independent: an interval lies in exactly one block, and the chosen intervals of one block must cover that block alone. Within a block the problem is the classic minimum cover of a segment by intervals. Start with the leftmost point of the block; the chosen interval must start there, and the best one is the one with the maximum end. Then repeat with the covered part extended: pick, among the intervals with a ≤ reach, the one with the largest b, as long as it extends the reach.

In code: sort by start; outer loop starts a new block at the next unprocessed interval, with reach = a; inner loop consumes every interval with start ≤ reach and takes the maximal end; if it exceeds reach count one more interval and continue, otherwise the block is complete. Every interval is consumed once, so after sorting the scan is linear: O(n log n) time, O(n) space.
